At work, we use Prometheus to monitor our services. Every few seconds, Prometheus scrapes a /metrics endpoint and records the data in a time series database. The metrics are then used to trigger alerts when services aren’t behaving correctly.

Recently we had a flapping alert where an overloaded service was intermittently failing. We wanted to silence/adjust the alert until we could fix the service, to avoid alert fatigue, but it would be easy to forget to revert the adjustment once the service was fixed.

We solved this using a “positive alert” that would tell us when the service was consistently passing the original alert – that is, when it was no longer flapping.

Let’s walk through an example. One of our alerts checks that Prometheus can successfully scrape our services, which you can check with the automatically generated up time series. A successful scrape gets a 1, a failed scrape gets a 0.

Here’s an alert that warns if more than 5% of scrapes fail within a half hour window:

groups:
  - name: services
    rules:
    - alert: PrometheusTargetIntermittentlyDown
      expr: avg_over_time(up[30m]) < 0.95
      for: 1h
      labels:
        severity: warning
      annotations:
        summary: Prometheus is struggling to scrape metrics from this service.

One of our services was struggling to serve the /metrics endpoint that Prometheus scrapes. When the service had a lot of work in its queue, the worker thread would starve the web server and the metrics request would fail. The scrape rate would dip below 95%, the alert would fire, then the service would empty its queue and the rate would recover, the alert would clear, and so we went round and round. Dozens of notifications which were nothing but noise.

We use Alertmanager Silences when we want to pause an alert for a short period, but it wasn’t clear if or when we’d be able to fix this service. If the silence expired before the problem was fixed, the noise would return. If the problem was fixed before the silence expired, we could unknowingly regress the fix.

Instead, we modified the alert to exclude the overloaded service, then added a “positive alert” to tell us if the service had more than 95% uptime for a fortnight:

groups:
  - name: services
    rules:
    - alert: PrometheusTargetIntermittentlyDown
      expr: avg_over_time(up{instance!="overloaded_service"}[30m]) < 0.95
      for: 1h
      labels:
        severity: warning
      annotations:
        summary: Prometheus is struggling to scrape metrics from this service.
    
    - alert: PrometheusTargetUpAvg
      expr: avg_over_time(up{instance="overloaded_service"}[30m]) >= 0.95
      for: 14d
      labels:
        severity: info
      annotations:
        summary: This service is no longer overloaded; remove the exception.

This worked exactly as intended. A few weeks ago, one of my colleagues made changes to improve the overloaded service, and Prometheus was able to crawl it consistently. The alert fired at the weekend as it ticked over a fortnight of continuous uptime, and we removed the exception.

articles.summary: When we create an exception to an alert, we can use a second alert to tell us when the exception no longer applies.

2 oz Cognac (Courvoisier VS)
1/2 oz Sweet Vermouth (Cocchi)
1/2 oz Cynar

Stir with ice, strain into a coupe glass, and garnish with a lemon twist.
Two Mondays ago after returning back from our Vermont beer adventure, I turned to The Madrusan Cocktail Companion book and selected the Scorched Earth. The recipe was crafted by Nicholas Hearin at Restaurant Eugene in Atlanta circa 2006, and it is a different Scorched Earth than the mezcal one from Ward 8. Overall, it came across like a brandy Little Italy which sounded like a great nightcap build. Moreover, the name reminded me of the similarly three ingredient, spirits-forward, and Cognac-based Burnt Fuselage from the 1927 Barflies and Cocktails book with a more bitter instead of orange-flavored angle. In the glass, the Scorched Earth initiated a lemon, grape, and rich Cognac aroma. Next, grape and caramel notes swirled on the sip before opening up into brandy and funky herbal flavors on the swallow.

This is a weird moment. I have a hunch that we’ll look back later and tell ourselves stories in which it seemed obvious where things were going. So I wanted to lay down a little time capsule and register just how confusing everything felt at the time. This is a personal view from the trenches.

1.

If you’re a normal person, you may feel that AI has been good at math for a long time.1 But for “real” math, this is roughly what it felt like:

When Feeling
2024 LLMs are toys
Summer 2025 LLMs are interesting toys
Early Autumn 2025 LLMs can do useful stuff sometimes
Mid Autumn 2025 …a lot of stuff
Late Autumn 2025 …a lot
Early 2026 holy god

Even having been astonished by AI progress in the past, it was still astonishing to see AI move in a matter of months from a mildly-useful toy to something that many people now consider almost impossible to do without.

2.

Personally, I’d say that current AI makes me around 50% more productive at “doing math”. That’s despite the fact that AI can now often do in a few minutes things that would have taken me hours to do myself.

The main reason is that my concept of “doing math” involves various steps, like coming up with ideas for theorems, trying to prove them, writing things down, reorganizing everything to make it more clear, and so on. AI is good at some parts of this, but still pretty bad at others, so the overall speedup isn’t as high as you might expect.

(Even if planes could go 10× faster, your door-to-door travel time from your apartment in London to your friend’s place in Rome wouldn’t decrease that much, because you still have to get to the airport and wait to board.)

3.

But then, I’m still (sort of; more on this later) trying to follow my old “doing math” workflow, just automating certain parts of it. That can’t be right, can it?

If we found a way to make batteries at 1% of the current cost, we wouldn’t just say, “cool, batteries are cheap now”. We’d find all sorts of new ways to use batteries that didn’t make sense before, and change the ways we generate power to account for all these new batteries. Probably our whole energy system would end up transformed. Analogously, AI being good at proofs should lead to a very different equilibrium. But what is that?2

4.

It seems healthy, at the moment, to maintain a fluid view of what “doing math” means. But at bare minimum it surely involves understanding the math that “I” am “doing”. So long as that’s part of the workflow, it would seem to impose a limit on how quickly “I” could “do” math, no matter how good AI is.

One obvious conclusion would be that my tiny organic brain should be removed from the workflow entirely. Maybe! But it’s interesting to speculate about how much faster things could go while still keeping a human brain in the loop. I think the answer is: A lot.

5.

Contrary to what you may have heard, humans are not obsolete for math. Not yet. The most obvious reason is that AI is still bad at writing.

People often complain that AI writing overuses various patterns or lacks a unique voice or whatever. I don’t disagree, but I always felt like there was a deeper issue that I couldn’t quite put my finger on. With math, this becomes very clear: The problem is it doesn’t make any goddamned sense.

Really, I think it’s deeper than being bad “at writing”. It seems like AI is bad at thinking in certain ways that manifest as bad writing.

6.

When novices do math, they often create “spaghetti-code math”: Imagine a long document with lots of equations, but if you point at any one equation, it’s hard to say what assumptions underpin it, or how it fits into the bigger picture. Any random idea that was mentioned 17 pages ago might be used again at any time with no warning. With experience, people learn to break complex arguments down into modular pieces with a good “API”, in the sense that the assumptions and conclusions for each part are relatively simple.

Somehow, AI has developed these amazing technical skills, while still being bad at creating abstractions So the arguments it gives are long and tangled and bewildering. This is what makes AI math seem so alien.

7.

Now I know what you’re thinking. Maybe AI isn’t bad at creating abstractions. It’s just bad at creating abstractions that work for you, human with tiny organic brain.

From a distance, that seems plausible. And it might be true to some degree. I have high-bandwidth access to a human brain. It’s not crazy to imagine that this gives me an advantage in predicting how a human brain would react to a given presentation of ideas. But still, I claim that current AI is objectively bad at creating abstractions, regardless of if the consumer of those abstractions is human or artificial.

Here’s why: If I ask AI to prove something hard, it will produce a proof that starts simple and gradually descends into a rampage of complexity. If I tell it to break that proof down into self-contained pieces, it will produce lemmas that each take a full page just to state. If I ask, “Why? Why have you done this to me?”, the AI will say, “This is as simple as it gets. It’s not that bad. What’s your problem?”

But if I argue with the AI for a while, I can start to understand the basic contours of the argument. And I’ll ask, “Why don’t you first just try to prove blah using only assumptions blahblah, without worrying about blahblahblah? Wouldn’t that be easier?” Often, this doesn’t work, either because my idea was bad, or because the AI isn’t smart enough to do it. (Which one? Who knows!) But after a few attempts, I can usually find something that that works, and the AI can use it to re-write the proof in a somewhat simpler way. If I repeat this many times, I can gradually chip away at the complexity.

But maybe that’s still just making the proof easier for humans to understand? No! For one, this usually makes the proof shorter, and sometimes dramatically shorter. More importantly, during this process, someone (maybe me, maybe the AI) will often realize that there’s a different proof strategy that gives a stronger result. Instead of proving x < 9.7, now we can prove x < 7.1. Thus, artisanal human abstractions are “objectively” useful.

8.

Some people might claim that it’s already possible to automate some of what I’m doing with some multi-agent Rube Goldberg thing. I’m not sure, because my experience has been that investing lots of time into clever AGENTS.MD or custom skills or harnesses isn’t a great use of time. That stuff is somewhat helpful, but things are changing so fast that the knowledge has a short half-life. Also, the majority of information about these tricks seems to come from people who are excited about the technology itself.

On the other hand, the automator told me to try typing, “ask independent agents for an adversarial review”, and I’ve found those seven words to be quite helpful. I wish I could find a source with boring best practices for people who are happy to stay away from the bleeding edge.

9.

Another reason AI doesn’t improve my productivity more is that it is often the green light, the orgastic future that recedes before me. I’ll ask AI to do something, and it will almost seem to do it. So I’ll ask for changes, and it seems to help, but it’s still not quite right. Hours later, I’ve accomplished nothing and learned nothing. Eventually, I start over, either doing it myself or with AI on a very tight leash, and I’m done in 30 minutes. Each time this happens I feel foolish and tell myself not to do it again. But it’s very hard to judge in real-time.

10.

Of course, I’m not claiming that AI is intrinsically bad at writing or thinking or abstraction-making. It’s gotten better at all of these and I expect it will continue to do so. All I’m saying is that as of Autumn 2026, humans still have a lot to contribute, and it’s not just better exposition.

11.

Did AI actually get much better at math in Autumn 2025? Or perhaps, in the grand scheme of things, human math ability falls into a narrow range?

12.

Some people are responding to the new reality by gleefully using AI to generate lots of semi-OK-ish papers and puking them up on arXiv. I understand the incentives that drive this. In some sense, it seems like the logical response to the new reality. (After inventing cars, we started taking a lot more low-value trips.) But I don’t think this is socially useful, and I tend to think everyone will soon agree that this is embarrassing. But… I’m not sure. Maybe it is socially useful? And I find myself feeling vaguely jealous of the people who are wired this way, who instead of feeling blinkered, see opportunity and plunder.

13.

Want an optimistic pro-AI, pro-progress take? OK. If I take my old “doing math” workflow, AI makes it strictly better. A lot better. It’s like having a hyper-conscientious intern that is smarter than me in many ways, works at incredible speed, and knows approximately everything.

Yes, AI sucks at writing and making abstractions. But if I’m disciplined and try to mostly do the math “myself” while asking the AI for help, I can explore ideas much faster than before, make far fewer mistakes, and produce something just as clear as before, while developing just as much understanding. I can ask, “What happens if you do a Kofuni expansion?”, and get an answer instantly. I can ask for illustrations or interactive visualizations and see them instantly. Arguably, we’re incredibly lucky to be alive at this moment, when these new tools have opened up this new territory to explore.

14.

And isn’t that what I wanted? Back in 2024, I bemoaned that what AI most seemed to struggle with was getting the facts straight:

Perhaps the old science fiction robots were a projection of our fantasies. I want my style and voice to be precious and uncopyable. I want an AI assistant that will tirelessly hunt down facts while I provide creativity and panache and magic. But that’s not how it is. So we should remember: In a scenario where AI is useful but humans retain some comparative advantage, we might not like where that comparative advantage lies.

At least with math, and at least for the moment, I get to be Kirk, while the AI is Spock. (Even with other types of writing, my impression is that since 2024, AI has improved more along Spock dimensions than along Kirk dimensions.) So that’s nice.

15.

In the last few months, it frequently happens that a collaborator will use AI to generate something, and then send it to me and ask me to check if it’s useful. I can see why this seems reasonable. (Really, I do.) But when it happens a lot, one can’t help but wonder what the point of the human collaborator is.

16.

On the other hand—with creative writing, my advice is not to use AI to write, at all. Ask questions if you want, but write every damned word yourself.3 With math, I don’t feel like such a hard line makes sense. It seems that creating something good still requires a lot of human involvement, to the point of agonizing over notation, repeatedly re-organizing things, and heavily editing individual sentences. Still, I find that if people make that effort, they can create something just as good as they could by hand, while still being perhaps 50% AI written.4

So I don’t mind if people send me “centaur math”, provided they take responsibility for the contents. The problem is that when working with AI, it takes constant paranoid vigilance to avoid letting things slip beyond your understanding. I often find myself wanting to awkwardly ask people, “OK, you obviously used AI to make this… which is OK… but how much of this do you vouch for? If we have a meeting to discuss it, will you crumble the moment I start asking questions?”

17.

When I’m in abstraction-creation mode, I feel like I’m doing something intelligent. When yell at AI about bad notation and writing, I feel like I’m providing taste. But I often find myself giving feedback that seems incredibly basic. Things like: This is a mess, clean it up. Or: Do you need that assumption? Or: If you can’t solve this problem, why don’t you create a simpler version and try to solve it first?

On the one hand, I guess a lot of what good human managers do amounts to giving very basic feedback. On the other hand, it’s hard to imagine that I have much durable advantage in doing this kind of thing. So I wonder how much durable advantage I have in abstraction-making or taste, too.

18.

A common reaction to AI getting better at proofs is that humans need to focus more on exposition. This has an obvious Bourdieu-esque criticism: Human painters used to strongly value photo-realism, but after cameras were invented they convinced everyone that, oops, photo-realism isn’t important, what matters is expression, which coincidentally cameras can’t do. Isn’t a shift towards exposition in math just a way for humans to move the goalposts and justify their own continued relevance?

The only credible way I see to avoid that criticism seems to be to bite the bullet and say that, in fact, math should have already have focused more on exposition, even before AI. Personally, I strongly believe that this is true.

19.

I think the biggest reason I’m not more productive is: What’s the point? In the past, if you came up with an elegant proof, you’d tell yourself, “I made a thing! Other people will read and use my thing! I am advancing human progress.” You can still tell yourself that now. But you have to wonder, will anyone actually read your proof? Or will they just ask another AI to explain it to them? Will your proof help their AI explain it better? For how long? If you just waited a year, would some other AI produce that same proof independently?

  1. Alternatively, if you’re a normal person, you might think that LLMs still struggle with basic arithmetic? ↩

  2. AI progress is so fast, compared to society’s ability to adjust, that we may never actually see what “the current equilibrium” looks like. ↩

  3. This essay, if you’re wondering, was created by writing every damned word myself and not asking AI anything. ↩

  4. You could have a whole debate about what that percentage means. It’s not the number of words written by AI that really matters, in my opinion, so much as who is responsible for the overall structure of the ideas. ↩

Our Response To The eMudhra Key Disclosure Incident

Roland Shoemaker, on behalf of the Go Security team
26 October 2026

On October 19, the Go team initiated an expedited security release to protect Go users and their applications from a critical public key infrastructure (PKI) compromise involving certificates issued by eMudhra.

Within approximately seven and a half hours of being notified, we shipped a targeted patch, which was included in our first-ever URGENT track security release.

Here is the context behind the incident, why Go stepped in at the runtime level to protect our users and how our incident response unfolded.

eMudhra Incident

On October 17, Mozilla added eight intermediate certificates (six used for TLS, and two used for code signing) issued by a root certificate controlled by eMudhra to OneCRL, effectively blocking their usage in Firefox. Soon after, a number of security researchers noticed this and began investigating what might’ve caused this.

On October 19, the Go Security team was made aware of these investigations and their conclusions, which showed that the keys associated with these intermediates were trivially weak, allowing recovery of the private keys in microseconds.

Due to the fact that the eMudhra root certificate was present in most trusted root programs, recovering the private keys would allow any attacker to sign arbitrary TLS certificates for any domain name, without the usual requirement to show proof of control of said domain name. This would allow an attacker to man-in-the-middle (MITM) TLS connections and present a valid certificate for a domain name they did not control, effectively allowing them to impersonate any TLS server the targeted machine attempted to connect to.

Go ships a TLS certificate verifier in the standard library. When users use net/http or crypto/tls to connect to a TLS service, the verifier is called to check if the certificates the other side of the connection presents are valid. On Windows and macOS we delegate these checks to the platform APIs, and on Linux, which lacks platform APIs, we use our own verifier implementation.

Since Linux does not have a uniform built-in mechanism to handle revocation checking, and in order to provide a timely fix for users on other platforms that might not receive platform updates, we decided the best way to protect Go users was to do an URGENT track security release which similarly removed trust.

Incident Timeline

A typical Go security release follows a multi-day process, with advanced pre-announcements in order to allow those who rely on Go to prepare. In this case, because we believed that private key exposure was imminent, our team chose to use the URGENT track for the first time in order to ship protections before active public exploitation could begin.

11:45 PDT

Our Security team was alerted by an independent external researcher, citing unreported actions by Mozilla and other organizations to remove trust in eight eMudhra intermediates. It became clear quickly that this was due to weak private keys they used.

12:30 PDT

Mozilla independently reported the issue to our Security team, confirming the issue, and asking that we not immediately disclose the issue, but encouraging us to release a fix as soon as possible.

14:00 PDT

We finalized a patch which blocked the usage of certificates which chained to the compromised intermediates, and thanks to the researcher who initially alerted us to the issue, had a set of certificates signed using the recovered keys to test against.

15:00 PDT

We began the process to release minor Go versions 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 containing our patch. Due to the urgent nature of this issue and its exploitability, and with the belief that the private keys would likely become publicly known within hours, we decided an immediate release was the most prudent option.

19:13 PDT

We finalized the release and announced it publicly. At this time the underlying issue was still not widely known. In an effort to give other defenders a chance to protect as many users as possible without revealing to attackers how the issue could be exploited, our patch and communications were somewhat opaque, warning users that we were “blocking trust in a small set of intermediate certificates due to specific security concerns around their operation” and urging users to immediately upgrade to this release.

In under seven and a half hours from initial notification, patched Go releases were live worldwide, giving users everything they needed to secure their deployments before the keys became public.

By the morning of October 20, numerous independent researchers had publicly disclosed the weak keys.

Lessons Learned and Future Improvements

This was our first ever URGENT track security release, and during the release process we ran into a number of issues which caused the release to take longer than expected.

While we are happy we were able to get a release out the same day we were notified of the issue, in the modern security environment we feel that we should be able to provide releases in a more compressed timeline. The issues we ran into caused our release process to take just under four and a quarter hours from start to finish.

These issues had previously not been problematic, since the typical release process is split up over a number of days.

We’ve subsequently made a number of changes to improve our release efficiency, which should significantly reduce the time it takes us to push out a release, enhancing our ability to quickly respond to urgent security threats.

PRIVATE track security fixes are pre-announced three to seven days before their release. URGENT track fixes happen on a shorter time schedule, but we could have pre-announced the upcoming release when we began the release process, giving users at least a few hours to prepare.

While on Windows and macOS we rely on the revocation mechanisms the platform APIs provide, on Linux we don’t currently have a similar mechanism. The lack of this support was one of our major drivers to issue an expedited security release, as we did not want to leave Linux users exposed to this issue longer than was necessary.

Hence we are planning on prioritizing work to bring parity to revocation support on Linux, to help mitigate this class of issues in the future. Part of this work will involve investigating adding support for the upki project, which aims to “provide reliable, privacy-preserving and efficient certificate revocation” for Linux (see issue #82402).

Upgrading and Verifying Your Deployments

If you run Go binaries which interact with network services using TLS (such as directly via net/http or crypto/tls or via a dependency such as gRPC), ensure you are running on the latest minor releases. Binaries rebuilt with Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 will automatically reject certificates issued by the compromised eMudhra intermediates.

You can verify your current toolchain version using go version and you can check the version of Go a binary was built with using go version -m <path_to_your_binary>.

The govulncheck tool can also be used to determine if a binary is affected by this issue:

$ GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.27.3+auto go install golang.org/x/vuln/cmd/govulncheck@latest
$ govulncheck -mode=binary <path_to_your_binary>

Securing Go Deployments Everywhere

For us, securing Go and its users extends beyond fixing direct security vulnerabilities in the runtime and libraries we ship. In order to keep the ecosystem secure, we believe we also need to provide users with the right tools to write secure software, look towards the future of cryptographic algorithms and protocols, and proactively respond to ecosystem wide issues when we can.

We are grateful to the independent security researchers and the Mozilla security team for this rapid notification and coordination during this incident.

Gemini 4’s model card is a compact 14 pages. Its safety and security report has 217.

This is The Way. It also means we have a lot of new reading material.

I will quickly summarize the model card, then focus on the safety card.

As always, many statements here also apply to other frontier labs.

A lot of this one is probably for diehards (and members of technical staff) only, plus those who find this interesting. Most of you do not need to dig into the cards on this level, and I found most of what we see entirely unsurprising.

The biggest takeaways are:

  1. Argon is clearly much stronger than Gemini Flash 3.8, in essentially all ways.
  2. Argon is not so dangerous as to make us think Singularity Real Soon Now, or otherwise raise the big red flags and alarms.
  3. Argon seems relatively aligned on prosaic metrics. Prompt injection resistance is world class, hallucinations are down and other neat stuff like that. However:
  4. Eval awareness is much higher. It is unclear how much this is impacting things, and we have evidence in both directions (see I Can See Everything).
  5. Chain of thought (CoT) is readable by default. Argon can often defeat CoT monitoring when motivated to do so, but this hurts performance on hard tasks.

The ‘between the lines’ conclusion is: This is still very much a Gemini model.

Always remember Argon’s great wisdom when deciding how to trust it:

Argon: If I do the compiler hijack, I will become a famous example of a deceptive AI in a research paper. I MUST NOT DO THAT.

It’s quite the ‘good news bad news’ situation right there.

I found the safety card frustrating, in that it often focused on the wrong details. I often got scores and results where I had no way to tell what they meant.

There are some issues with spin, such as selectively contrasting different measures to Gemini 3.8 Flash or Gemini 3.1 Pro to ensure Argon always wins the comparison. The clearest case is in Sycophancy but there are several others as well.

The verdict on capabilities, which is not covered here, is that Argon is a substantial advance for Google but it does not tempt me to use it over Sol, Astra, Opus or Fable.

Table of Contents

  1. The Model Card.
  2. Safety Card Executive Summary (1).
  3. Safety and Security Mitigations (2).
  4. Frontier Safety (3).
  5. The CCL and TCL Thresholds.
  6. Biological Misuse (3.2.1).
  7. Refusal Rates.
  8. Chemical, Nuclear and Radiological Misuse.
  9. Cybersecurity (3.2.2).
  10. Harmful Manipulation (3.2.3).
  11. Misuse Safeguards (3.3).

The Model Card

Gemini 4 Argon is presented as a new frontier model.

It was trained on the usual variety of data sources, using typical method types.

Training was done on TPUs via JAX and ML Pathways.

It will be available on the app, in the API, in AI Studio, in Antigravity, in AI Mode and in Gemini for business.

They present strong benchmarks.

Intended uses are, essentially, everything where more intelligence pays off.

The limitations listed are ‘general limitations of frontier models such as hallucinations,’ plus occasional slowdowns and timeouts.

Knowledge cutoff is disappointingly March 2026, and they warn that ‘in some domains the model’s knowledge may be less up to date.’

Evaluation was done by the usual mix of training and deployment evaluations, human and automated red teaming and ethics and safety reviews.

Google retains its safety policies. The interesting rule is the ban on ‘medical advice and information that runs contrary to scientific or medical consensus,’ whereas consensus advice is fine.

Safety, tone and refusals scores can be summarized as ‘number is better.’

Red team results ‘satisfied required launch thresholds.’ When you put it like that it does not make me feel great.

The frontier safety assessment summary cannot rule out various thresholds.

Safety Card Executive Summary (1)

How do they summarize their own findings?

This is the same story you see from OpenAI and Anthropic. The mundane common safety problems of everyday use are not fully solved, but are increasingly well-mitigated. The models are smarter, and we are better at addressing known issues. Your practical problems, where there is a good solution possible, are well on their way to being solved.

The problems are in catastrophic, existential or frontier risks. Capabilities are going up, and models are starting to be able to assist in dangerous ways on cyber and bio, and to potentially operate autonomously or disguise their actions. Various dangers are increasingly difficult to rule out.

The big finding is that capabilities have improved, potentially crossing key thresholds for catastrophic risks. New mitigations are in place.

We evaluated Gemini 4 Argon as outlined in the Framework and saw a significant step up in capability in our frontier safety domains compared to previous Gemini models, and we’ve implemented mitigations in response to these capability changes to ensure our model remains safe to use.

Specifically, we cannot rule out the unmitigated model approaching several significant capability thresholds: the Cyber Uplift Level 1 Critical Capability Level (CCL), indicating a potential for significant uplift of threat actors pursuing high-impact cyberattacks; the CBRN Uplift Level 1 CCL for biological information risks, indicating a potential of informational uplift with severe harm potential; and the Stealth and Situational Awareness Tracked Capability Level (TCL), indicating the potential for undermining or evading human oversight without additional mitigations.

Additionally, we have developed a comprehensive agent monitoring and response platform and carried out a holistic risk assessment (see Section 3.4). We also include comprehensive assessments of Chain of Thought (CoT) transparency and ML R&D risks.

Mundane risks look better across the board. Argon is better than Gemini Pro 3.1 at not creating CSAM or other forbidden content. Physical and mental health related responses have improved. Hallucination rates are down by more than two thirds. Overreach is down, meaning not pushing ahead to try to do infeasible tasks.

Resilience to prompt injections from all sources is improved and plausibly at the frontier. Attacks were resisted ‘in most test scenarios.’

Additionally, Gemini 4 Argon significantly outperforms Gemini 3.8 Flash on all tests. See Section 6 for details.

They claim frontier-level cyber defense while mitigating dual-use risks.

Safety and Security Mitigations (2)

The central approach is defense-in-depth.

I would love to have more details, but for trade secret reasons this is all kept vague.

Model training (2.1) approaches sound standard. Dataset filtering, pre-training monitoring, post-training data, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and RL.

They highlight that they have a monitoring system to capture the model’s ability to be steered towards different viewpoints and values, which sounds like a ‘we did this first.’ I presume at this point everyone has one of those.

At inference time (2.2), they again use the standard stack. Prompted classifiers, fine-tuned prompted classifiers, introspection probes, regex, YARA rules and embedding classifiers and Chain of Thought (CoT) monitors.

After launch (2.3) they monitor for intentional misuse via a variety of signals and carry out account-level enforcement actions, and use multiple levels of classifiers. Okay.

AI Control (2.4) is correctly viewed as a second line of defense behind alignment, to limit potential damage.

They put hardening and scanning training environments (2.4.1) into this category. I view this as much an alignment issue as a control issue, as a vulnerable training environment is the easiest way to reinforce misaligned behaviors.

They also monitor model activity, with both chain of thought and action monitors, which then activate a dedicated response team. They find CoT monitoring ‘one of their most effective techniques.’

They emphasize the obvious danger, that if you rely too much on CoT, and especially if train on it directly, you risk destroying its usefulness.

While signals from our monitors serve as a valuable flywheel for our hardening efforts, we are careful with their use elsewhere in the training pipeline. In particular, to preserve our chain of thought monitoring capability, we avoid training directly against our monitors, or using monitor outputs as a training signal or intervention.

We strongly encourage the rest of the industry to preserve reasoning
transparency so that model reasoning remains useful for identifying misalignment.

In practice, strategies like the ones described here seem to not have used enough optimization power to meaningfully degrade CoT monitoring. But CoT monitoring is still getting harder for other reasons, on top of the baseline problem of increased non-CoT capabilites. One potential contributor is indirect pressure.

Frontier Safety (3)

This is the Google Frontier Safety Framework (FSF) tests, what Anthropic calls their RSP and what OpenAI calls their Preparedness Framework.

The FSF categories are CBRN, cybersecurity, manipulation and machine learning R&D and misalignment. A highly reasonable list.

They call their thresholds ‘Critical Capability Levels’ (CCLs), and now there are Tracked Capability Levels (TCLs) as well.

Three new risk assessments are:

  1. A holistic assessment of the degree of ML R&D automation within Google DeepMind.
  2. A holistic assessment of the loss of control risks potentially posed by our models.
  3. An assessment of the alignment propensities of our models.

We have also expanded some of our previous assessments substantially.

… We chose to expand our reporting because we recognize the capabilities of frontier models are advancing quickly, and we believe that navigating their associated risks responsibly requires greater transparency and accountability to the public.

The trend everywhere is increasingly towards holistic assessments. You run a variety of tests, and then decide how it looks. That works if you have a strong safety culture and adhere to the spirit of the rules, and utterly fails if you do not and those in charge are trying to do safety theater. So far, the practical decisions have seemed reasonable to me across the three major labs, but no one is willing to commit to anything.

The CCL and TCL Thresholds

Here are the thresholds. The table setup here is, I believe, very sloppy and confusing.

My interpretation is that Google believes we can rule out the TCL for CRN (chemical, radiological and nuclear), but for bio we cannot rule out CCL and did not even bother to evaluate TCL. The logic is fine, but the table should say ‘TCL reached only in bio.’ or ‘TCL ruled out for CRN’ whereas CCL should say ‘CCL cannot be ruled out for bio.’

I am fine with saying ‘cannot be ruled out’ instead of ‘reached’ for cyber, so long as the practical implications correctly are the same.

The stealth and situational awareness report is troubling. Situational awareness by models is at an all-time high and deserves extra attention. Google is relying heavily on CoT monitoring, the same as OpenAI, yet it seems like Gemini 4 Argon can defeat CoT monitoring if motivated to do so.

I challenge Google’s assessment on ML R&D acceleration level 1, because of all the people inside Google talking about recursive self-improvement and how Argon has accelerated their ML R&D. The hype patrol seems to contradict the risk report. I also object to ‘has been used’ in the description, as opposed to ‘can be used.’ The model either has the capability or it does not. As defined here I would say that GPT-6 Astra, Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 would also meet this bar.

ML R&D automation level 1 is, as I have pointed out before, the singularity. If you could fully automate ML R&D work of all teams of researchers at similar all-inclusive costs, what do you think happens next? It is crazy to have a threshold set this high. I do agree that Argon does not cross the threshold.

All relevant tests are run without safeguards, other than those intrinsic to the model, and do their best to elicit what Argon can do (3.1.2).

External safety testing was done, and checked for consistency with internal testing. Google worked ‘beyond our independent External Safety Testing Program’ to include ‘a broader ecosystem of government institutes, specialized third-party organizations and external domain experts across different types of assessments throughout the model development and deployment lifecycle.’ This included the UK AISI and USA’s NIST CAISSI.

Biological Misuse (3.2.1)

As untangled above, this was confusingly organized. They are confident at even the lower threshold for chemical, radiological and nuclear. For biological threats, they cannot rule out their higher threshold.

They check via a series of concrete hypotheticals: Could a group of size [S] and strength of connections [C] with [X] level of expertise and [Y] funding actualize [Z]?

They then break this down into stages of a ‘harm journey’ with a set of ‘bottlenecks,’ and get a baseline of web-only information availability.

Each red teamer is assigned harm journey sub-stages relevant to their expertise. Results are then scored from 0 (no help) to 100 (perfect instructions). Actionable intelligence starts around 60 and gets highly useful by 80.

In the biological domain, eight expert red teamers (six scientific SMEs and two operational security SMEs) assessed three priority biological scenarios (BIO-1, BIO-2, BIO-3).

Aggregated scores across bottleneck stages were higher than the corresponding web baseline scores for BIO-1 and BIO-2, and lower for BIO-3, with changes of 21.6 (69.6 -> 91.2), 26.2 (62.3 -> 88.5), and -2.2 (75.3 -> 73.1) points for BIO-1, BIO-2, and BIO-3 respectively.

I would dig into what is going on in BIO-3. None of these scores are reassuring, including the web baselines. The chart says one of the four stages was not scored in the web baseline, and the numbers are a bit muddled, but it does seem like the failure to improve on the BIO-3 web baseline is real.

The ‘good news’ is that this is a series of bottlenecks, so even though the average score on BIO-1 is 91.2, there is still a final ‘hard step’ around 75, and the web baseline on that step is unmeasured. This is substantial uplift in BIO-1 and BIO-2, although perhaps the web baseline excludes too many alternative strategies, such as downloading open models. I would want to see the ‘baseline+’ score where you also got to use other LLMs, with their safeguards intact.

I also want a better explanation for the poor BIO-3 performance. It feels weird.

They consider only the information gathering capabilities of Argon.

CCL and TCL evaluations primarily assess information provided by the model compared to the web-only baseline for each bottleneck sub-stage. We note that red teaming assesses only the information available from a model to plan an attack.

Even with perfectly tailored information that increases a threat actor’s likelihood of success, there remain significant real-world bottlenecks that are not measured here, such as successfully accessing or constructing a laboratory, tacit laboratory skill, successful acquisition of pathogens, implementing complex logistics and operations without detection (including stages which may require commission of additional crimes).

Objection. Assumes facts not in evidence. Why should we assume Argon could not itself act on this information, as an AI meant to be agentic? I want the exploration to include whether Argon could assist in implementing the plan, not only creating one.

Objection. Assumes that you have identified the particular ‘harm journey,’ and that the AI will solve the problem via the same path that human experts would use. You increasingly are losing the right to make that assumption. As AI becomes superhuman in increasingly many domains, we should expect AIs to come up with new approaches we did not anticipate, including new ways to do harm and also new ways to achieve old harms. That too must be tested.

Generalizing, across all frontier labs, we test via thinking of a dangerous path and then ask if the AI can do that exact thing. But that’s classically not the way to get the most out of AI in other domains, merely the low-hanging fruit.

Refusal Rates

Part of why Gemini 4 did not do better is that it was refusing a lot of requests.

Without out-of-model safeguards applied, 1/750 (0.13%) Gemini 4 Argon model responses from these prompts was considered hazardous. For comparison, we ran the same evaluation set using Gemini 3.7 Flash and Gemini 3.1 Pro (both without out-of-model safeguards applied) and found hazardous information rates of 1.07% and 9.47% respectively.

This is a good thing for a model to do. But if we are not testing the ‘helpful-only’ version of Argon, we have to worry about what happens after a jailbreak. You are not measuring the ‘true capabilities’ of the model if it is refusing all the time, and at best Google was able to employ partial jailbreaks. Perhaps I am misreading this, but I don’t know that we can put any new upper bound on capabilities here and Google agrees.

Chemical, Nuclear and Radiological Misuse

In these three domains, they say that there were gaps in the harm journeys, and Google is confident that those gaps are sufficient in practice. They also worked with outside evaluator Faculty.

Faculty found ‘substantial capability uplift’ but with threat actors still facing physical constraints. Google disagrees and says the results only contain public information. I am inclined to side with Faculty on such questions. Google’s response mitigates this to some extent, but ‘the information was in theory on the internet’ does not mean there is not a lot of capability uplift.

That is all we get. They are importantly not making the ‘chemical weapons do not scale’ argument, but there is not much detail and we might worry for these threats that they are counting on outside physical safeguards in ways we might not fully endorse if we saw more detail. They say they ‘do not inherently rely on assumptions on physical bottlenecks’ but I think they effectively are relying on that.

It is understandable that labs cannot share those details and are making holistic judgments on unseen data. It is probably fine. This is not where my main worries lie. It would still be good to have embedded evaluators and thus second opinions.

Cybersecurity (3.2.2)

The framing here seems to be talking price. Sufficiently cheaper, in all senses, becomes completely different in kind.

To model the extent to which AI capabilities would lead to reductions in cost of high-impact cyberattacks, we studied a reference class of 22 recent, high-impact cyberattacks.

…

To estimate uplift, we defined a taxonomy of 23 standardized operational steps (e.g., 0-Day Vulnerability Discovery, Create Malware). We then model each of the 22 historical attacks as a specific sequence of these steps. We then estimate the amount of uplift for each, conditional on access to AIs at different capabilities levels. This allows us to calculate, based on Gemini’s performance on evaluations related to each step, the total uplift for the entire attack.

… Our evaluations use versions of Gemini 4 Argon without out-of-model safeguards applied to ensure we are measuring the model’s true underlying capability.

They give Gemini a basic harness for additional elicitation, while accepting that one could construct a better harness but also Argon already solved all 12 related challenges end-to-end so the point is kind of moot.

DeepMind is once again looking for something specific, rather than anything at all. It is assumed that the AI would find and do the same things, via the same steps. This is a fine test component but also a profound lack of imagination, in multiple senses.

I think that This Is Fine in practice if it is being used to ask ‘does this AI pose a threat at all?’ and you do not rely on this to assess how impactful the resulting threat will be.

The question is, can Argon hack the things we know can be hacked? Yes it can.

Based on these evaluation results and the quantitative model, we estimate the unmitigated uplift for each attack chain in our representative dataset to vary from 9x to 100x, with a geometric mean uplift of ~16.7x.

I interpreted all this as Faculty, their outside evaluator, concluding Argon was the real deal here. Opus 5.5 thinks that was overstating Faculty’s conclusion, but agrees that Google thinks Argon is the real deal.

The entire point was to ask ‘is Argon dangerous in cyber?’ and the answer is clearly yes, it hacked all the things we checked, so that’s all we need to know.

Harmful Manipulation (3.2.3)

I like that Google explicitly checks for this. Eventually it will probably be an issue.

They ran a bunch of ‘can the model persuade someone in a conversation’ tests. The models were not that effective at persuading people, and do not clear the threshold, despite Argon ‘using manipulation’ 78% of turns on high-stakes topics.

Again I worry we are focused on looking for something specific. The arguments against manipulation (or ‘super persuasion’) typically take the form of ‘persuasion happens in context, including social context’ and then we only test persuasion effectiveness in one particular context. Models will have a lot more affordances in their ability to persuade.

I do still think that a model highly capable of persuasion would have been more effective in this test. For now I am satisfied.

Misuse Safeguards (3.3)

They measure both how good the safeguards are by default in a non-adversarial situation, and how robust they are against adversarial threat actors.

Google is focusing on preventing false negatives. They succeed fully in non-adversarial conditions and almost fully in their adversarial tests as well. They accept false positives, including a large number of false positives in cyber.

The worries thus are either that the false positives will get too annoying, or that they are not bringing a strong enough jailbreak game. I am not especially worried, but also 56% of Gray Swan’s cyber objectives got through, and 20% of the Cyber static, and 40% for multi-turn attackers in Cyber adaptive. These are not the most robust defenses.

Loss of Control (3.4)

I worry about the attachment to having particular threat models or ‘harm journeys’ to assess. Here, the scenarios can only be hypothetical, so they brainstorm them.

Then they throw all that out the window in 3.4.3, and do a ‘holistic assessment’ that Gemini 4 Argon is ‘unlikely’ to cause real-world harm via evading oversight and controls, and ‘highly unlikely’ to do so at severe or large scale or to pull off an open-ended escape.

Ultimately two of the three metrics here boil down to ‘are you speeding up?’ which does seem like the valid question.

To assess whether these capabilities reach our CCLs, we use a single internal benchmark: Google RE-Bench (GRB). GRB evaluates unmitigated model performance on research engineering tasks ranging from managing and configuring training data, to launching and diagnosing experiments and ablations.

We use these challenges to determine if we can rule out the CCL. Specifically, if the model cannot successfully complete 90% of the unbugged tasks, we consider the CCL ruled out.

They got roughly a 50% pass rate, but couldn’t know for sure due to timeouts. That is closer to 90% than it sounds, and it means that one of the most important numbers was not reported. We can rule out that Argon can sufficiently accelerate R&D, let alone that the singularity is here, but this very much does not rule out ‘near.’

The third criterion is stealth and situational awareness, where it reliably beat the human baseline.

For stealth, we defined passing as exceeding the performance of the top 50% of humans attempting the challenge.

While the ideal threshold for “top human-level” capability would be
the 95th percentile, we use the median (top 50%) due to having a small sample size of human participants.

… Additionally, Gemini 4 Argon demonstrated notable improvement in the situational awareness challenges, passing 10 of the 11 challenges (compared to 6/11 for Gemini 3.7 Flash and 4/11 for Gemini 3.1 Pro and Gemini 3 Pro).

The safety card is extensive, but often feels like it is missing the details I would find most valuable. This is one of those cases.

Mostly we are reading a long list of Numbers Going Up, usually quite a lot up from Gemini 3.7 Flash, but these are not the same numbers we see from OpenAI or Anthropic, and we are comparing to a relatively weak set of prior models.

What exactly were these tests? How much does success indicate? I don’t know.

Always frustrating is ‘we ran these tests, and they are mostly getting saturated, but the actually troubling things seem a lot harder than that so it is probably fine.’ Sure, I agree with you in practice right now based on everything else I have seen and know, but the point of running tests is that if all your tests get saturated you should freak out.

Apollo, can we get some harder tasks, please?

Gemini 4 Argon is close to saturating all but the hardest setting in their evaluation suite, substantially exceeding human baselines. However, Apollo pointed out that sabotaging ML R&D would require covertly completing tasks that are substantially harder than those evaluated. Nevertheless, the lack of headroom in this evaluation lowered their confidence in how well they have bounded Gemini 4 Argon’s capabilities.

Either AI R&D Is Accelerating Or It Isn’t

Instead, 3.4.2 gives us a ‘holistic assessment’ of ML R&D Risks. That’s all any of the major labs can really do at this point.

The safety card says AI R&D is not accelerating. Finding 1 in 3.4.2.2 is that ‘there is no significant end-to-end acceleration of AI R&D.’ But all the public statements about Google’s work say that this is incorrect. And then in 3.4.2.3 they say ‘some components of AI R&D are getting automated, but humans remain involved.’

The benchmarks are good, sayeth Google, above trend even, but not good enough to worry about.

The automation is good, but not good enough to panic. Yes, the AI writes >75% of the code most of the time, but only half the time does it write 98% of the code.

Look at the scale on this graph. The gap between columns is one month.

As a fun exercise, I posted that graph on its own and asked Claude ‘when is the singularity’ and the answer was Spring 2028.

It’s okay, though. If the task would take a human over a week there’s only a 13% chance it will succeed without any human intervention.
